title-group.article-title: Therapeutic role of semaglutide in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis: A systematic review and meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials with GRADE evidence assessment

sec.title: Background:
sec.p: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and its progressive form, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), are leading causes of chronic liver disease worldwide. Despite the rising clinical burden, there are currently no approved pharmacologic therapies. Semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist with established metabolic and weight-loss benefits, is being evaluated for potential disease-modifying effects in NAFLD/NASH.

sec.title: Objective:
sec.p: To assess the efficacy and tolerability of subcutaneous semaglutide versus placebo in adults with NAFLD or NASH, focusing on biochemical, histologic, metabolic, and safety outcomes.

sec.title: Methods:
sec.p: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of placebo-controlled randomized controlled trials evaluating subcutaneous semaglutide in adults (≥18 years) with NAFLD or NASH diagnosed by imaging, histology, and/or biochemical markers. PubMed, CENTRAL, and Scopus were searched from inception to May 15, 2025 using predefined terms related to semaglutide and fatty liver disease. Two independent assessors extracted data and evaluated risk of bias using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, while certainty of evidence was appraised with Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation. Pooled effect estimates were calculated using a random-effects model and reported as risk ratios (RRs) or mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Semaglutide significantly reduced liver enzymes, including aspartate aminotransferase (MD = −6.72 U/L, 95% CI = −11.79 to −1.64; P = .009). Histologically, semaglutide more than doubled the likelihood of NASH resolution without fibrosis progression (RR = 2.14, 95% CI = 1.44–3.17; P = .0002). Improvement in fibrosis stage was not statistically significant (RR = 1.14, 95% CI = 0.63–2.05; P = .67), though the direction of effect favored semaglutide. Metabolic outcomes showed substantial benefits, including weight loss (MD = −6.99%, 95% CI = −13.92 to −0.06; P = .05) and improved glycated hemoglobin (MD = −1.29%, 95% CI = −1.46 to −1.13; P < .00001). Gastrointestinal adverse events and treatment discontinuation occurred more frequently with semaglutide, while serious adverse events were comparable to placebo (95% CI = 0.81–1.41; P = .64; P = .65).

sec.title: Conclusion:
sec.p: Semaglutide demonstrates promising efficacy for NASH resolution and meaningful metabolic improvement with an overall acceptable safety profile. Its effect on fibrosis remains uncertain, and longer-term, adequately powered trials are needed to clarify its role in NAFLD/NASH treatment.
Keywords: GRADE, meta-analysis, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, randomised controlled trials, semaglutide, systematic review
Received 2026 Jan 8; Revised 2026 Jul 1; Accepted 2026 Jul 9; Collection date 2026 Jul 24.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: According to an extensive worldwide meta-analysis, nearly 33% of people are affected by nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), which is now recognized as the most common long-term liver disease.[1] Multiple epidemiologic studies confirm that nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) has overtaken other causes, becoming the leading reason for chronic liver disease and a rapidly growing contributor to liver cirrhosis globally.[2] The American Liver Foundation also states that NAFLD is “the most common cause of liver disease worldwide,” with NASH as its more aggressive form.[3] Recent data suggest that NAFLD affects about one-quarter of adults worldwide,[4] with rising prevalence linked to increasing rates of type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity.

NAFLD ranges from simple steatosis to NASH, which can develop to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular cancer.[5–9] Despite its rising impact and serious health repercussions, no pharmaceutical medicines for NASH have been authorized yet, underscoring the urgent need for safe and effective therapeutic options.[10–13]

As a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA), semaglutide has been shown to improve metabolic health by lowering blood glucose levels and promoting weight loss in patients with type 2 diabetes and obesity. These benefits, along with new preclinical and clinical evidence, suggest that semaglutide might also have disease-modifying effects in NAFLD and NASH. Several randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have recently examined semaglutide in this context, evaluating both histologic and biochemical outcomes.

A meta-analysis published in 2023 combined evidence from RCTs and nonrandomised studies to examine semaglutide’s role in NASH and NAFLD.[14] However, that analysis encompassed trials featuring active comparators (e.g., cilofexor, firsocostat),[15,16] diverse study designs,[17–19] and heterogeneous patient populations,[16] potentially introducing considerable variability and constraining the interpretability of its conclusions regarding semaglutide’s independent efficacy.

Recognising these limitations, we conducted a methodologically rigorous meta-analysis focused on placebo-controlled RCTs evaluating semaglutide in adults with NAFLD or NASH. This narrower focus makes it easier to evaluate how semaglutide affects clinically important endpoints, such as aspartate aminotransferase (AST), histological resolution of steatohepatitis without fibrosis progression, alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and fibrosis improvement. In addition, our analysis incorporates newly published trials, such as the large phase 3 ESSENCE study, which were not available to earlier reviews.

By addressing previous methodological limitations and incorporating recent high-quality evidence, our study aims to provide an updated and comprehensive assessment of the safety and effectiveness of semaglutide compared to placebo in treating NAFLD and NASH. We believe this synthesis fills a vital evidence gap and may inform clinical practice and guideline development.

sec.title: 1.1. Compliance with reporting guidelines
sec.p: This article complies with the TITAN 2025 guidelines on the declaration and use of artificial intelligence tools in scholarly publishing.[20]

sec.title: 2.1. Registration and protocol
sec.p: Our research followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines[21] to ensure clarity. The protocol was also prospectively registered in the PROSPERO database (registration ID: CRD420251081804), which promotes reproducibility and supports future research.

sec.title: 2.2. Databases and search approach
sec.p: Up to May 15, 2025, we conducted systematic searches in PubMed, Scopus, and CENTRAL. Searches used both MeSH terms and free-text keywords for semaglutide and NAFLD/NASH. We used trial and design terms to find randomized, placebo-controlled trials. The search terms included (“Semaglutide” [Supplementary Concept] OR Ozempic OR semaglutide OR Wegovy OR “Glucagon-Like Peptide 1 Receptor Agonists” [MeSH]) AND (“Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease” [MeSH] OR “Steatohepatitis, Nonalcoholic” [MeSH] OR NAFLD OR NASH OR nonalcoholic fatty liver OR nonalcoholic steatohepatitis OR “Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease” OR “Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatohepatitis” OR MASLD OR MASH). Only human studies and reports published in English were included; 2 independent reviewers deduplicated and assessed the records. Detailed search strategy is presented in Table S1, Supplemental Digital Content 1.

sec.title: 2.3. Eligibility criteria
sec.p: The eligibility criteria included RCTs that were placebo-controlled and parallel-group, involving adults (≥18 years) with NAFLD or NASH diagnosed through imaging, histology, or biochemical markers. The intervention of interest was subcutaneous semaglutide at any dose or frequency compared to placebo. Studies were excluded if they were nonrandomised, single-arm, or post hoc analyses; if both arms used semaglutide; if relevant outcomes were not reported; or if the full text was not available in English.

sec.title: 2.4. Data collection
sec.p: Two authors independently collected information using a pretested Microsoft Excel form. The extracted variables included study details and baseline population characteristics. The evaluated outcomes encompassed biochemical parameters, histological endpoints, metabolic indices, and adverse events. Any disagreements between authors were resolved through consensus and discussion.

sec.title: 2.5. Assessment of risk of bias
sec.p: The quality of the included RCTs was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 (RoB 2) framework.[22] Five domains were evaluated: randomization process, missing outcome data, deviations from intended interventions, measurement of outcomes, and selective reporting. Each domain was rated as minimal risk, some concern, or elevated risk. Review Manager software (RevMan v5.4; The Cochrane Collaboration) was employed to generate summary and traffic-light plots. Disagreements were resolved through reviewer discussion until consensus was achieved.

sec.title: 2.6. Evidence certainty
sec.p: Evidence quality was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) framework along with the GRADEpro Guideline Development Tool.[23] Two reviewers independently evaluated the evidence and graded it as high, moderate, low, or very low.[24] Any disagreements in assessment were resolved through discussion and consensus.

sec.title: 2.7. Statistical analysis
sec.p: A random-effects model was used in all pooled analyses to account for variability across studies. Dichotomous outcomes were expressed as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), while continuous variables were reported as mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs. We assessed statistical differences among studies using the I2 statistic, considering values above 50% as substantial. All statistical calculations were performed in Review Manager (RevMan) version 5.4.

sec.title: 2.8. Ethical consideration
sec.p: This study is a meta-analysis of previously published aggregate data. Therefore, no institutional review board approval was required, and informed consent was not applicable, as this study did not involve direct patient contact, primary data collection, or any intervention. All analyses were based on de-identified, publicly available data from previously published studies, which were conducted in accordance with the ethical standards of their respective institutional review boards and the Declaration of Helsinki.

sec.title: 3.1. Search results
sec.p: A total of 307 records were identified, and 27 duplicates were removed. After automated filtering excluded 86 ineligible records, 194 studies were screened by title and abstract. Of these, 156 were excluded, leaving 38 articles for full-text review. Finally, 4 placebo-controlled RCTs were included in this meta-analysis. The study selection process is summarized in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses flow diagram (Fig. S1, Supplemental Digital Content 2).

sec.title: 3.2. Study and baseline characteristics
sec.p: This meta-analysis combined 4 RCTs: Flint et al,[25] Newsome et al,[26] Loomba et al,[27] and Sanyal et al.[28] The included trials were conducted in multiple countries, with durations ranging from 48 to 72 weeks. Sample sizes ranged from 22 to 343 participants. The mean age ranged from 54 to 61 years, and the proportion of male participants varied from 25% to 73%. Studies included both individuals with or without diabetes, where the proportion of type 2 diabetes ranged between unreported and 75%. Baseline body weight was consistently high (95–105 kg), and liver enzymes and fibrosis markers were abnormal, indicating active liver disease.

Semaglutide was administered subcutaneously at doses ranging from 0.1 mg once daily to 2.4 mg once weekly. All trials evaluated changes in liver enzymes, histologic and metabolic markers, and safety outcomes. Study details are summarized in Table S2, Supplemental Digital Content 3. Patients were mainly middle-aged and obese, with frequent type 2 diabetes. Baseline ALT, AST, liver stiffness, and enhanced liver fibrosis scores were elevated across the studies, indicating steatohepatitis and fibrosis. Detailed patient characteristics are provided in Table S3, Supplemental Digital Content 4.

sec.title: 3.3. Risk and bias assessment
sec.p: Risk of bias assessments for the included studies are shown in Figure S2, Supplemental Digital Content 5. Three trials (Flint et al, Loomba et al, and Sanyal et al) had a low risk of bias across all 5 domains. One trial (Newsome et al) was rated as “some concerns” due to issues in outcome measurement. In total, 75% of the studies were assessed as carrying low risk (Fig. S2, Supplemental Digital Content 5).

sec.title: 3.4. Grade assessment
sec.p: The GRADE method was used to assess the certainty of evidence for the outcomes comparing semaglutide to placebo. Evidence for primary histological outcomes, including resolution of steatohepatitis without worsening of fibrosis and reduction in liver fibrosis without worsening of steatohepatitis, was rated as moderate quality, primarily due to heterogeneity. Evidence for glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) reduction and safety outcomes, including treatment-emergent adverse events, discontinuations, and severe adverse events, was considered of high quality, reflecting robust and consistent findings. Outcomes related to liver stiffness and serum cholesterol were graded as moderate quality because of variability and wide CIs. In contrast, AST and weight reduction were rated as low quality, and ALT levels received a very low-quality rating due to high heterogeneity (I2 > 90%) and imprecision. Gastrointestinal adverse events (diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting) showed consistent, high-quality evidence of increased risk. No serious concerns regarding indirectness or publication bias were identified. A detailed GRADE summary of findings is available in Table S4, Supplemental Digital Content 6.

sec.title: 3.5.1. Effect on AST levels
sec.p: Across 3 studies, 293 participants were analyzed (157 received semaglutide, 136 placebo). Pooled results indicated a significant reduction in AST with semaglutide versus placebo (MD = −6.72 U/L, 95% CI = −11.79 to −1.64; P = .009), though heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 92%; Fig. 1).

caption.p: Forest plot comparing the effect of semaglutide versus placebo on AST levels in adults with MASLD or MASH. AST = aspartate aminotransferase, CI = confidence interval, MASH = metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, MASLD = metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, SD = standard deviation.

sec.title: 3.5.2. Effect on ALT levels
sec.p: Three studies comprising 294 participants (158 on semaglutide, 136 on placebo) were analyzed. Semaglutide produced a larger decrease in ALT than placebo (MD = −10.75 U/L, 95% CI = −22.14 to 0.65), but the effect was not statistically significant (P = .06). Heterogeneity was marked (I2 = 98%; Fig. 2).

caption.p: Forest plot comparing the effect of semaglutide versus placebo on ALT levels in adults with MASLD or MASH. ALT = alanine aminotransferase, CI = confidence interval, MASH = metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, MASLD = metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, SD = standard deviation.

sec.title: 3.5.3. Resolution of steatohepatitis without worsening of liver fibrosis
sec.p: A total of 985 patients were included across 3 studies (semaglutide: 637; placebo: 348). Semaglutide significantly increased the chance of resolving steatohepatitis without worsening liver fibrosis compared to the placebo (RR = 2.14, 95% CI = 1.44–3.17; P = .0002). Heterogeneity was moderate (I2 = 47%), indicating some variability among studies but overall consistent effects (Fig. 3).

caption.p: Forest plot showing the effect of semaglutide versus placebo on resolution of steatohepatitis without worsening of liver fibrosis. CI = confidence interval.

sec.title: 3.5.4. Reduction in liver fibrosis without worsening steatohepatitis
sec.p: Across 3 studies, 975 participants were enrolled (semaglutide: 627; placebo: 348). Semaglutide did not show a significant benefit over placebo in reducing liver fibrosis without worsening steatohepatitis (RR = 1.14, 95% CI = 0.63–2.05; P = .67). Significant heterogeneity was observed (I2 = 75%), indicating substantial variability between studies (Fig. 4).

caption.p: Forest plot showing the effect of semaglutide versus placebo on improvement in liver fibrosis without worsening of steatohepatitis. CI = confidence interval.

sec.title: 3.5.5. Effect on liver stiffness
sec.p: Three studies involving 246 participants (131 on semaglutide, 115 on placebo) were analyzed. Pooled results indicated no significant improvement in liver stiffness with semaglutide versus placebo (MD = −0.82 kPa with 95% CI = −1.99 to 0.35; P = .17). Considerable heterogeneity was detected (I2 = 78%), reflecting study-level variation (Fig. 5).

caption.p: Forest plot comparing the effect of semaglutide versus placebo on liver stiffness measurements in adults with MASLD or MASH. CI = confidence interval, MASH = metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, MASLD = metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, SD = standard deviation.

sec.title: 3.5.6. Percent weight reduction
sec.p: Across 3 trials, 1029 participants were enrolled (semaglutide: 650; placebo: 379). The combined analysis showed that semaglutide resulted in a significantly greater percentage of weight loss compared to placebo (MD = −6.99%, 95% CI = −13.92 to −0.06; P = .05). However, heterogeneity was very high (I2 = 99%), indicating substantial variability among studies (Fig. 6).

caption.p: Forest plot comparing the effect of semaglutide versus placebo on percentage body weight reduction. CI = confidence interval, SD = standard deviation.

sec.title: 3.5.7. Effect on serum cholesterol levels
sec.p: Three studies comprising 300 patients (163 on semaglutide, 137 on placebo) were analyzed. Pooled findings showed a larger reduction in serum cholesterol with semaglutide versus placebo (MD = −6.17 mg/dL, 95% CI = −16.26 to 3.91), though the difference was not statistically significant (P = .23). Heterogeneity was minimal (I2 = 0%), reflecting consistency among trials (Fig. 7).

caption.p: Forest plot comparing the effect of semaglutide versus placebo on serum cholesterol levels. CI = confidence interval, SD = standard deviation.

sec.title: 3.5.8. Effect on serum HbA1c
sec.p: Across 3 studies, 215 participants were enrolled (semaglutide: 121; placebo: 94). The pooled analysis demonstrated that semaglutide significantly lowered serum HbA1c compared to placebo (MD = −1.29%, 95% CI = −1.46 to −1.13; P < .00001). Heterogeneity was very low (I2 = 3%), indicating consistent results across studies (Fig. 8).

caption.p: Forest plot comparing the effect of semaglutide versus placebo on HbA1c levels. CI = confidence interval, HbA1c = glycated hemoglobin, SD = standard deviation.

sec.title: 3.5.9. Treatment-emergent adverse event
sec.p: A total of 1493 patients were included across 4 studies (semaglutide: 961; placebo: 532). The pooled analysis showed that semaglutide was associated with a slightly higher risk of treatment-emergent adverse events compared to placebo (RR = 1.09, 95% CI = 1.04–1.14; P = .0004). There was no heterogeneity (I2 = 0%), indicating highly consistent results across studies (Fig. 9).

caption.p: Forest plot comparing the incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events between semaglutide and placebo groups. CI = confidence interval.

sec.title: 3.5.10. Effect on serum triglycerides
sec.p: Only one trial (Sanyal et al) reported absolute mean changes in serum triglyceride concentrations. In this phase 3 study, the semaglutide group experienced a mean reduction of −16.77 mg/dL compared with −0.27 mg/dL in the placebo group, yielding a between-group difference of −16.54 mg/dL (95% CI = −21.02 to −11.81). The remaining trials reported triglyceride outcomes as ratios of follow-up to baseline or as estimated treatment ratios without baseline means. Consequently, a pooled MD could not be calculated.

sec.title: 3.5.11. Adverse events leading to discontinuation
sec.p: Three studies collectively enrolled 1422 participants (semaglutide: 914; placebo: 508). The pooled analysis showed no significant difference between semaglutide and placebo in adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation (RR = 0.87, 95% CI = 0.48–1.58; P = .65). There was no heterogeneity (I2 = 0%), indicating consistent results across studies (Fig. 10).

caption.p: Forest plot comparing adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation between semaglutide and placebo groups. CI = confidence interval.

sec.title: 3.5.12. Severe adverse events
sec.p: Across 4 studies, 1493 participants were analyzed (semaglutide: 961; placebo: 532). The pooled analysis showed an RR of 1.07 (95% CI = 0.81–1.41; P = .64), suggesting a 7% increased risk of severe adverse events with semaglutide, although this was not statistically significant. There was no heterogeneity (I2 = 0%), indicating consistency across the studies (Fig. 11).

caption.p: Forest plot comparing the incidence of severe adverse events between semaglutide and placebo groups. CI = confidence interval.

sec.title: 3.5.13. Diarrhea
sec.p: Four studies together enrolled 1493 participants (semaglutide: 961; placebo: 532). The pooled analysis showed an RR of 1.98 (95% CI = 1.54–2.54; P < .00001), indicating a significantly higher 98% risk of diarrhea with semaglutide. Heterogeneity was absent (I2 = 0%), demonstrating consistent findings across studies (Fig. 12).

caption.p: Forest plot comparing the incidence of diarrhea between semaglutide and placebo groups. CI = confidence interval.

sec.title: 3.5.14. Nausea
sec.p: Four studies together enrolled 1493 participants (semaglutide: 961; placebo: 532). The pooled analysis showed an RR of 2.88 (95% CI = 2.27–3.65; P < .00001), indicating a significantly higher risk of nausea with semaglutide. There was no heterogeneity (I2 = 0%), demonstrating consistent results across studies (Fig. 13).

caption.p: Forest plot comparing the incidence of nausea between semaglutide and placebo groups. CI = confidence interval.

sec.title: 3.5.15. Vomiting
sec.p: Four studies together enrolled 1493 participants (semaglutide: 961; placebo: 532). The pooled analysis revealed an RR of 3.70 (95% CI = 2.47–5.54; P < .00001), indicating a significantly increased risk of vomiting associated with semaglutide. No heterogeneity was observed (I2 = 0%), indicating uniform results across studies (Fig. 14).

caption.p: Forest plot comparing the incidence of vomiting between semaglutide and placebo groups. CI = confidence interval.

sec.title: 3.6. Causes of high heterogeneity
sec.p: Significant heterogeneity was observed for ALT (I2 = 98%) and weight loss (I2 = 99%) outcomes. This variation likely results from differences in trial design, including semaglutide dosing (ranging from 0.1 mg to 2.4 mg/week), study durations (48–72 weeks), and participant factors such as baseline liver enzyme levels, metabolic comorbidities, and fibrosis severity. Trials involving patients with more advanced liver disease or lower baseline ALT may have exhibited weaker treatment effects, contributing to the observed differences.

Although nausea did not significantly differ between semaglutide and placebo (RR = 1.07; P = .64), it remains one of the most common gastrointestinal side effects. In studies, nausea usually occurred during the dose-escalation phase and was temporary and mild. Differences in how symptoms were reported and classified might explain the lack of statistical significance, even though vomiting and diarrhea showed consistent increases.

Semaglutide caused weight loss in both diabetic and nondiabetic groups. Although some trials with more diabetic participants showed larger absolute reductions, the overall trend stayed consistent across different metabolic backgrounds, confirming semaglutide’s effectiveness in weight control.

sec.title: 4. Discussion
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis provides a comprehensive evaluation of the efficacy and safety of semaglutide in patients with NAFLD, recently renamed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and its inflammatory subtype, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH/MASH). Overall, the pooled evidence indicates that semaglutide leads to meaningful improvements in key histological and biochemical features of NASH, although its effect on liver fibrosis remains uncertain.

The most notable finding of this analysis is that semaglutide significantly increases the likelihood of resolving steatohepatitis without worsening liver fibrosis (RR = 2.14; P = .0002). This represents an important therapeutic advance, as histological resolution of NASH is a recognized surrogate endpoint for regulatory approval and is associated with improved long-term liver-related outcomes.[29,30] These results are consistent with the established mechanisms of GLP-1 RAs, which improve steatohepatitis through multiple pathways, including enhanced insulin sensitivity, reduced lipotoxicity, and direct anti-inflammatory effects within the liver.[26,31] A recent meta-analysis by Zhu et al further supports these findings, demonstrating a significantly higher rate of NASH resolution with semaglutide, along with improvements in steatosis, lobular inflammation, and hepatocellular ballooning.[32,33] The moderate heterogeneity observed in our analysis likely reflects differences in study design and patient populations, including variations in baseline metabolic characteristics and dosing regimens.[26]

In contrast, semaglutide did not demonstrate a significant benefit for the endpoint of fibrosis improvement without worsening of steatohepatitis (RR = 1.14; P = .67). The substantial heterogeneity for this outcome (I2 = 75%) suggests that treatment response may be influenced by factors such as baseline fibrosis stage, duration of therapy, and patient comorbidities. These findings indicate that while semaglutide is highly effective in targeting the metabolic and inflammatory drivers of NASH, its direct impact on the fibrogenic process may be limited or may require longer treatment durations to become apparent.[34] This distinction is clinically important, as fibrosis stage remains the strongest predictor of liver-related mortality in NAFLD.[35] The lack of a significant improvement in liver stiffness, a noninvasive marker of fibrosis, further supports this observation.

These results align with the known biological effects of GLP-1 RAs. Preclinical studies have shown that semaglutide modulates key metabolic and inflammatory pathways, leading to reduced hepatic expression of genes involved in inflammation and fibrogenesis.[33] In addition, semaglutide has been shown to inhibit pro-inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-α and interleukin-6, decrease hepatic lipid accumulation, and enhance β-oxidation, thereby addressing several core metabolic abnormalities underlying NASH.[33,36] The beneficial hepatic effects of semaglutide likely reflect pleiotropic mechanisms. Beyond its GLP-1 receptor-mediated effects on appetite regulation and glucose homeostasis, semaglutide has been shown to reduce hepatic inflammation, improve insulin sensitivity, modulate lipid metabolism and β-oxidation, and attenuate pro-fibrotic signaling.[33]

The biochemical outcomes provide further insight into the hepatoprotective effects of semaglutide. The significant reduction in AST levels (MD = −6.72 U/L; P = .009), along with a strong trend toward ALT reduction (MD = −10.75 U/L; P = .06), supports improvements in hepatic inflammation. However, the very high heterogeneity observed for these outcomes limits their interpretability. This variability is likely attributable to differences in dosing strategies, study duration, and participant characteristics, including baseline liver enzyme levels and diabetes status.[37,38]

The therapeutic benefit of semaglutide in NASH is closely linked to its favorable metabolic effects. Significant reductions in body weight and HbA1c represent key advantages of GLP-1 RA therapy. Weight loss, particularly in the range of 7% to 10%, has been strongly associated with NASH resolution and improvements in fibrosis.[11] The extremely high heterogeneity observed for weight reduction (I2 = 99%) likely reflects variability in background lifestyle interventions, dosing, and patient adherence across studies. Nevertheless, the overall findings consistently reinforce semaglutide as a potent agent for metabolic control in this patient population. The observed reduction in serum cholesterol, although not statistically significant in this analysis (P = .23), follows a favorable trend and is consistent with the known lipid-modifying effects of GLP-1 RAs.[26,39]

The safety profile observed in this analysis aligns with the well-established class effects of GLP-1 RAs. Semaglutide was associated with a modest but statistically significant increase in overall treatment-emergent adverse events (RR = 1.09; P = .0004), primarily driven by gastrointestinal side effects. The risks of diarrhea (RR = 1.98), nausea (RR = 2.88), and vomiting (RR = 3.70) were significantly higher in patients receiving semaglutide. These adverse events are typically dose-dependent, occur most frequently during the dose-escalation phase, and are generally transient and mild to moderate in severity.[13,14] Importantly, there was no significant difference between semaglutide and placebo in the rates of severe adverse events or treatment discontinuation due to adverse effects. This suggests that, although gastrointestinal symptoms are common, they are usually manageable and rarely necessitate treatment cessation, which is reassuring for routine clinical use.[15] However, one meta-analysis has reported a higher incidence of major adverse events with semaglutide, particularly related to gastrointestinal and gallbladder disorders.[14]

sec.title: 4.1. Assessment of publication bias
sec.p: Because our meta-analysis included only 4 trials, we did not perform formal statistical tests for publication bias. The Cochrane Handbook notes that funnel plots and associated asymmetry tests are unreliable when fewer than 10 studies are available. Therefore, we did not calculate asymmetry statistics; any visual assessment should be interpreted with extreme caution given the limited power of such methods in small‐study scenarios.

sec.title: 5. Limitations
sec.p: Several important limitations should be acknowledged. The relatively short duration of the included trials, ranging from 48 to 72 weeks, limits the ability to assess the long-term durability of histological improvements and their impact on clinically meaningful outcomes such as cirrhosis and mortality. In addition, there was considerable heterogeneity across studies, as different trials used varying semaglutide doses and incorporated differing levels of lifestyle intervention. The study populations also tended to have strict eligibility criteria, which may not fully reflect the broader and more heterogeneous NAFLD population encountered in routine clinical practice, thereby limiting the generalizability of the findings.

sec.title: 6. Conclusion and clinical implications
sec.p: This meta-analysis provides strong evidence that semaglutide is effective in achieving resolution of steatohepatitis in patients with NASH, likely driven by its substantial benefits in weight reduction and glycaemic control. However, its effect on liver fibrosis remains unclear and warrants further investigation. The safety profile of semaglutide is manageable and consistent with its known class-related effects.

Taken together, these findings position semaglutide as a foundational therapeutic option for NASH, particularly in patients with coexisting obesity and type 2 diabetes. Its use should be incorporated into a comprehensive management strategy that emphasizes lifestyle modification. Future studies should prioritize longer follow-up periods, optimization of dosing strategies, and exploration of combination therapies with antifibrotic agents to address the ongoing unmet need for effective fibrosis reversal in advanced NASH.
